extractor.prompt: Extract inheritance engagements: where Husserl engages predecessors on time-consciousness and intentionality in Bernau manuscripts
extractor.note: Partial pass focused on the editors' introduction. Identifies engagements with Brentano (restitution of doctrine, inner consciousness), Meinong (differences on retention), and later assistants/editors (Heidegger, Fink, Ingarden, Stein) who worked with the manuscripts. The Bernau texts notably contain no engagement with earlier contemporary theorists (James, Stumpf, Stern) who shaped Husserliana X.

coverage_note: Covers editors' introduction and programmatic engagements. Full pass would require examining the six main text groups (Texts 1-22) for detailed phenomenological engagements with predecessors.

engagements.claim: Husserl in the Bernau texts returns near to Brentano's doctrine of inner consciousness, which Husserl had always regarded sympathetically despite critical distance.
engagements.quote: A first leads him back near Brentano's well-known doctrine of inner consciousness, for which Husserl had already shown much sympathy despite all criticism.

engagements.claim: Husserl differentiates substantively from Brentano's understanding of retention as an act of re-presentation or categorical synthesis.
engagements.quote: He differed substantively from Brentano and Meinong in that he understood retention neither as an act of (phantasy-like) re-presentation nor as a categorical act of subsequent synthesis, but rather as a modality of perceiving itself.

engagements.claim: Like Brentano, Meinong's theory of retention is rejected in favor of retention as a modality of perception itself.
engagements.quote: He differed substantively from Brentano and Meinong in that he understood retention neither as an act of (phantasy-like) re-presentation nor as a categorical act of subsequent synthesis, but rather as a modality of perceiving itself.

predecessor.author: Brentano
predecessor.text: Phenomenology of time-consciousness and inner consciousness

engagements.claim: The Bernau manuscripts aim at a phenomenological deepening and restitution of the Brentano-Aristotelian doctrine of time and inner consciousness.
engagements.quote: a "restitution of the Brentano-Aristotelian doctrine" in phenomenological deepening, furthermore the diagram, the individuation-problematic leading already toward "transcendental logic," including the doctrine of the temporality of ideal objects.

predecessor.author: Heidegger
predecessor.text: Editorial publication and interpretation of Husserl's time-manuscripts

engagements.claim: Heidegger's 1928 publication and editorial introduction brought the earlier time-manuscripts to public attention and created expectations for the Bernau manuscripts.
engagements.quote: The editors note that less than half of the published text actually derives from the 1904/05 lectures; portions come from 1909–1911 research manuscripts, and still others from the 1917 redaction. The critical edition in Husserliana X documented the various working phases.

predecessor.author: Stein, Edith
predecessor.text: Compilation and redaction of time-consciousness dossier

engagements.claim: Edith Stein's compilation of the time-consciousness dossier in summer 1917 was the immediate occasion for Husserl's renewed engagement with time in the Bernau period.
engagements.quote: In July 1917 she apparently completed the compilation. In September 1917, she reports to Ingarden that Husserl is now working intensively on time in Bernau.

predecessor.author: Fink, Eugen
predecessor.text: Editorial preparation and systematic ordering of Bernau manuscripts

engagements.claim: Husserl entrusted the Bernau manuscripts to Fink for editorial preparation, regarding them as his main work; Fink sorted and organized them by formal criteria.
engagements.quote: Husserl regarded these manuscripts so highly that in 1927 he described them to Roman Ingarden as "my main work" (*mein Hauptwerk*). From 1926, Husserl unsuccessfully sought students to prepare the material for publication. Later, Eugen Fink (Husserl's personal assistant from August 1928\) was entrusted with the task.

engagements.claim: Ingarden was in correspondence with Husserl about the time-consciousness work and was considered for editorial preparation of the Bernau manuscripts.
engagements.quote: In September 1927, Husserl turned to Ingarden with the idea that he should prepare the Bernau manuscripts for print. Ingarden could not comply.

predecessor.author: James, William; Stumpf, Carl; Stern, William
predecessor.text: Theories of time-consciousness in Husserliana X period

engagements.claim: The Bernau manuscripts notably contain no direct engagement with the contemporary time-theorists (James, Stumpf, Stern) who shaped Husserl's earlier time-consciousness work in Husserliana X.
engagements.quote: Through engagement with Brentano, Meinong, James, Stumpf, Stern, and others (the Bernau manuscripts, notably, contain no engagement with these thinkers), Husserl came to the conviction that while perception of a lasting object normally occurs in a lasting act of perception, the duration of perception does not yet explain how the perception of an objective duration is possible.
